section_summary: This section concerns American sales of machinery and proposed steel plant contracts in Japan in 1939. State Department correspondence discusses the transfer of a Wooster, Ohio, machine shop, press reports about the sale, public objections, and the Department’s response to further proposed contracts. The section ends with a China Information Service bulletin criticizing the transfer and reporting on the war in China; several bulletin pages appear again as duplicates.

subfiles.title: Conversation on United Engineering and Foundry Company’s Japanese contracts
subfiles.about: A company representative asks about the risk of future export embargoes for Japanese steel mill contracts.
subfiles.summary: Arensberg describes existing and prospective mill contracts in Japan. Hornbeck declines to predict future restrictions and warns that new commitments carry increasing political risk.

subfiles.title: Marian Spence’s letter protesting the Wooster factory transfer
subfiles.about: A Seattle correspondent asks whether a reported factory transfer to Japan is true and urges a halt to war material shipments.
subfiles.summary: Spence quotes a press report alleging that a Wooster factory and American credit aided Japanese munitions production. She condemns American material support for Japan’s war in China and urges presidential action.

subfiles.title: Referral of Marian Spence’s letter to the Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department refers Spence’s factory transfer inquiry to Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Spence’s letter and the State Department’s reply for Commerce’s consideration.

subfiles.title: Reply to Marian Spence on the factory report and Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department refers her factual inquiry to Commerce and explains the limits of the 1937 Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost says Commerce is better placed to address the factory report. He explains that an arms embargo under the Neutrality Act would apply to both parties to a declared conflict.

subfiles.title: Coordination and Review routing note to Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Explains routing of correspondence and how Hornbeck and Green can receive relevant items.
subfiles.summary: Promises improved routing and asks Hornbeck to send correspondence through Coordination and Review.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s request to see all items in the file
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks to review all correspondence concerning a case in which he participated.
subfiles.summary: Notes unseen items and apparent gaps in enclosure numbers; requests future routing through him.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s note to Welles on the International News Service story
subfiles.about: Hornbeck reports that a Commerce Department source says a press service exaggerated his account.
subfiles.summary: Urges Welles to review the letters and proposed reply; identifies Commerce as the story’s source.

subfiles.title: Law firm’s correction of the Wooster factory press report
subfiles.to: Department of State, for Mr. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: The firm challenges a report that the factory sale proceeded over State Department objections.
subfiles.summary: The writer disputes the reported “oral remonstrances” and says Hornbeck gave no direct advice against the sale. The transferred machine shop is being dismantled and will not operate in Japan until 1940; the firm says it makes mill equipment and machine tools, not armaments.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s reply to Patterson, Crawford, Arensberg & Dunn
subfiles.about: Hornbeck addresses the inaccurate press story and clarifies his earlier remarks about the sale.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck agrees with the firm’s recollection and doubts that the story came from State. He says his remarks implied Departmental regret at such transactions.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversations on proposed Japanese manufacturing plants
subfiles.about: Arensberg seeks immediate guidance on contracts to replace German suppliers of Japanese plants.
subfiles.summary: Lind relays Arensberg’s inquiry after war in Europe disrupts German contracts. Green, after consulting Hornbeck, offers no further legal or policy advice. Arensberg then describes possible paint, steel rail, and armor plate plants and says his company will accept orders it can fulfill and collect on.

subfiles.title: China Information Service, Issue 30
subfiles.about: A bulletin reports Chinese war developments and criticizes the American factory transfer to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The issue reports Chinese gains near Changsha, peace rumors, a Japanese Foreign Office strike, and Chinese anniversary celebrations. Myron E. Terry argues that transferring the Wooster machinery factory helps Japan continue its war in China. It also reproduces Kiyokatsu Sato’s argument that war with the United States is inevitable, summarizes damage to Chinese higher education, and lists recent articles on East Asian affairs.

subfiles.title: Duplicate excerpt from China Information Service, Issue 30
subfiles.about: Repeated bulletin pages cover the Wooster factory, a predicted Japan–U.S. war, and part of the bibliography.
subfiles.summary: These pages repeat the Terry article and Sato extract from pages 104–107, then repeat the opening of the bibliography from page 109. The copy ends partway through the bibliography on page 115.
